prompt.context: Our client is the Houston Police Department. They have hired us to determine how many police officers they will need next year.
prompt.question: How many police officers will the Houston Police Department need next year? Walk through your analysis in four parts: (1) what factors would you analyze to estimate officer needs, (2) where would you find that information, (3) quantitative analysis, and (4) recommendations to improve efficiency if headcount cannot be increased.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current population of Houston?
clarifying_info.a: City population was 2 million in 2000, grew 20% between 2000 and 2007 to 2.4 million, and is expected to be 2.5 million in 2008.

clarifying_info.q: How has the city area changed?
clarifying_info.a: City area was 4,200 square miles in 2000, 4,400 in 2007, and is expected to grow 80 square miles by 2008 (to 4,480).

clarifying_info.q: What is the current officer-to-population ratio?
clarifying_info.a: Officers per 100,000 inhabitants: 220 in 2000 and 200 in 2007.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a benchmark from comparable cities?
clarifying_info.a: Los Angeles has 240 officers per 100,000 inhabitants.

exhibits.title: Houston Police Department Key Data Table
exhibits.shows: A table comparing city population, area (square miles), officers per 100,000 inhabitants, and number of officers across three years: 2000, 2007, and 2008 (estimated). The 2008 officer count is left blank for the candidate to calculate.

framework: Geography & statistical context: city population trends, area growth, population density
Labor & workforce factors: hours per week, days off, holidays, job type mix (administrative, traffic, crime prevention)
Crime and demand drivers: current and historical crime rate, special events, contingency scenarios
Benchmark analysis: officer ratios at comparable cities, crime rate comparisons, officer count evolution over time
Quantitative sizing: derive officer count from population ratio, then stress-test against benchmark
Efficiency levers: if headcount is constrained, identify operational, citizen-engagement, and resource-focus improvements

questions.prompt: Part 1 – What factors should be analyzed to estimate the number of officers needed? Organize into groups.
questions.guidance: Strong answer groups factors into at least three buckets. Expected buckets: (1) Geography & statistical info (city area, population, crime rate, number of police offices/stations); (2) Labor info (hours per week, days off, holidays, job types such as administrative, traffic control, crime prevention); (3) Other specific info (special planned events, contingency events); (4) Benchmark analysis (crime rate, officer count, job types, historical evolution in comparable cities).

questions.prompt: Part 2 – Where would you find the information for each factor identified?
questions.guidance: Candidate should map each bucket to a source. Geography/statistical info: local government statistics and PD data, obtained from the Administrative Chief. Labor info: head of HR or department staffers. Special events/contingency: senior leadership such as the Chief of Police. Benchmark: other city police departments (non-competitive, likely collaborative). Supplementary: interviews with community members about perceptions of safety.

questions.prompt: Part 3 – Using the data provided, calculate the number of officers needed in 2008. Then compare to the LA benchmark ratio of 240 per 100,000 and assess whether that benchmark is appropriate.
questions.guidance: Candidate should complete the table, identify the trend (ratio declining while population grows), then use a reasoned ratio to project 2008 needs. Should critically assess the LA benchmark rather than accepting it blindly.

math.setup: Population 2008 = 2,500,000. Officers per 100,000 ratio options: current 2007 rate (200), year-2000 rate (220), LA benchmark (240). Number of officers = (population / 100,000) x ratio.
steps: Using LA benchmark of 240: (2,500,000 / 100,000) x 240 = 25 x 240 = 6,000 officers
Using year-2000 ratio of 220: (2,500,000 / 100,000) x 220 = 25 x 220 = 5,500 officers (recommended)
Verification of 2007 figure: 2,400,000 / 100,000 x 200 = 24 x 200 = 4,800 officers
Verification of 2000 figure: 2,000,000 / 100,000 x 220 = 20 x 220 = 4,400 officers
math.answer: Recommended estimate: ~5,280–5,500 officers using the year-2000 ratio of 220 per 100,000. The LA benchmark of 6,000 is likely too aggressive — it implies a 25% increase in one year when population growth is ~1% annually, and LA's higher ratio may reflect historically high crime rates and greater geographic spread rather than a relevant peer comparison.

questions.prompt: Part 4 – If the PD cannot increase headcount, what recommendations would you give to improve efficiency and service?
questions.guidance: Strong answer organizes ideas into distinct buckets (at least three). Expected buckets and ideas below.

brainstorming.prompt: If the Houston PD cannot increase the number of officers, what ideas would you recommend to improve efficiency and service quality? Please organize by category.

categories.name: Operations
ideas: Analyze and streamline internal procedures to eliminate waste
Assess workload distribution across each division
Rebuild or rebalance teams if current structure is suboptimal

categories.name: Citizen Engagement
ideas: Educate and train the public on how to work cooperatively with police
Organize community seminars in neighborhoods to better understand local needs and concerns

categories.name: Resource Focus & Prioritization
ideas: Analyze crime rates by neighborhood to identify hotspots
Concentrate resources in highest-priority areas to maximize impact
Assess overall city needs and ensure resources are allocated to the most critical issues

categories.name: Staff Development & Technology
ideas: Assess individual officer strengths and match them to appropriate job types
Provide targeted training to increase officer effectiveness
Analyze current technology infrastructure and invest in IT improvements to reduce administrative burden

recommendation: Hire approximately 5,280–5,500 officers by 2008, restoring the year-2000 ratio of 220 per 100,000 inhabitants, rather than adopting the LA benchmark of 240 which would require an unrealistic 25% one-year increase
If budget constraints prevent full hiring, implement the efficiency measures across operations, citizen engagement, and resource focus simultaneously to maintain service quality
risks: Population and crime trends may diverge from projections, requiring an updated estimate mid-year
Comparing to LA may be misleading given differences in crime history and geography; a broader multi-city benchmark should be validated
Efficiency measures alone may not compensate for a significant officer shortfall if crime rates rise
next_steps: Validate benchmark by broadening the comparison set to 3–5 cities with similar population size and crime profiles
Conduct internal workload audit by division to identify reallocation opportunities
Develop a phased hiring plan tied to budget cycles and population growth milestones
